questions.q: What exact relationship did Kepler discover when he analysed the planets' distances and periods in 1618?
options: A planet's distance from the sun is directly proportional to its orbital period
The cube of a planet's mean distance from the sun is proportional to the square of its orbital period
The square of a planet's mean distance is proportional to the cube of its orbital period
A planet's speed is constant and identical for every planet in the solar system
questions.explanation: Kepler found that r³ ∝ T², so r³/T² is the same constant for every planet orbiting the sun. Option A (simple proportionality) is exactly the 'trap' the narrator warns against: Saturn is ~9.5× further than Earth but its year is ~30× longer, not 9.5×. The exponents are cubed-distance over squared-period, not the reverse.

questions.q: Why did Kepler think he was 'dreaming' when he looked at his table of numbers?
options: Every planet gave a different, random value with no pattern at all
The value of r³/T² came out to nearly the same number for all six wildly different planets
The planets turned out to orbit the Earth after all, confirming the old model
He realised the planets moved in perfect circles rather than ellipses
questions.explanation: Six independent worlds, from scorched Mercury to frozen Saturn, all gave r³/T² ≈ 7.5, agreeing to within a fraction of a percent — a single hidden law nobody had ever seen. Option D is wrong: Kepler's first law had already shown the orbits were ellipses, not circles; this third-law moment was about the distance–period ratio.

questions.q: Whose decades of precise naked-eye observations gave Kepler the data he needed to test his law?
options: Nicolaus Copernicus
Isaac Newton
Tycho Brahe
Galileo Galilei
questions.explanation: The Danish nobleman Tycho Brahe, famous for his silver nose and island observatory, measured planetary positions more accurately than anyone in history using giant metal instruments and his trained eye — all before the telescope. Copernicus proposed the sun-centred model but did not supply this data; Newton came decades later to explain the law.

questions.q: Why was the heliocentric model of Copernicus still not widely accepted before Kepler's work?
options: It could not predict planetary positions accurately, because it still assumed circular orbits
It failed to explain the retrograde (backwards) motion of Mars
There was no data available to test any model of the sky
It placed the Earth, not the sun, at the centre of the solar system
questions.explanation: Copernicus kept the ancient assumption that orbits must be perfect circles, so his predictions drifted from reality and were no better than the old model. Science runs on prediction, not beauty. Option B is wrong: the sun-centred picture actually explained retrograde motion elegantly (we overtake outer planets on a faster inner track).

questions.q: In the geocentric (Earth-centred) model, retrograde motion — a planet appearing to stop and loop backwards — was explained by:
options: Elliptical orbits with the Earth at one focus
Epicycles, small circles riding on larger circles, tuned by hand
The gravitational tug of one planet on another
The Earth overtaking outer planets on a faster inner orbit
questions.explanation: To rescue the Earth-centred theory, astronomers bolted on epicycles — wheels within wheels — tuned by hand to roughly reproduce the observed positions. Option D is the heliocentric (sun-centred) explanation of retrograde motion, not the geocentric one, and it is the correct modern picture.

questions.q: How did Kepler treat the small discrepancies in his table (Mercury's ratio slightly high, Saturn's slightly low)?
options: He fudged the data to make every value identical
He concluded the law was false and abandoned it
He accepted them as honest results of imperfect instruments and mutual gravitational tugs between planets
He ignored Saturn and Mercury entirely to keep only the clean values
questions.explanation: Kepler recognised that Tycho's instruments were not flawless and that planets gently tug on one another, nudging orbits away from perfect ellipses — so the tiny discrepancies were the fingerprints of a real universe, not a failure of the law. He did not fudge, abandon, or discard data.

questions.q: Why was Kepler's third law such powerful evidence for the sun-centred model?
options: It proved the planets move in circles as the ancients demanded
The Earth-centred model gave no reason to expect any distance–period relationship, yet here was an exact universal law that only makes sense if planets orbit the sun
It was the first idea that was more beautiful than the geocentric model
It allowed Kepler to calculate the mass of the sun directly
questions.explanation: The old Earth-centred model predicted no link at all between a planet's distance and its period, but Kepler found an exact, universal law that only makes sense if planets truly circle the sun, ruled by something reaching from the centre. Beauty (option C) was never the deciding factor — the script stresses science runs on prediction.

questions.q: Who later explained WHY Kepler's third law must be true, and with what idea?
options: Copernicus, using the assumption of circular orbits
Tycho Brahe, using more precise measurements
Isaac Newton, showing the law drops out of universal gravitation
Galileo, using observations through his telescope
questions.explanation: Kepler found the empirical footprint but could not say what caused it. Decades later Newton showed the law follows inevitably from universal gravitation — the same force that pulls an apple down reaches out to hold Saturn in orbit. Kepler found the footprint; Newton found the creature that made it.

questions.q: Using the constant from Kepler's data, k = r³/T² = 7.50×10⁻⁶ AU³/day², predict the orbital period T of Mars, whose mean distance from the sun is r = 1.524 AU.
given: Kepler's third law: r³/T² = k (a constant for all planets)
Mean distance of Mars: r = 1.524 AU
working: Rearrange r³/T² = k for the period: T² = r³ / k
Divide by the constant: T² = 3.540 / (7.50×10⁻⁶) = 4.72×10⁵ day²
Take the square root: T = √(4.72×10⁵) ≈ 687 days
questions.explanation: Rearranging r³/T² = k gives T = √(r³/k). With r = 1.524 AU, r³ = 3.540, so T² = 3.540/7.50×10⁻⁶ ≈ 4.72×10⁵ and T ≈ 687 days — matching Tycho's measured value of 686.95 days. This shows one constant predicts every planet's period from its distance alone.

questions.q: How is Kepler's third law still used by engineers today? Give a concrete modern application described in the episode.
keyPoints: The relationship r³ ∝ T² is used to place satellites in the correct orbit
It tells engineers precisely what altitude gives a desired orbital period
A geostationary satellite is placed so its period matches one turn of the Earth, hanging motionless over one spot on the equator
Used for television, weather, and navigation satellites
questions.explanation: Four centuries on, the same distance-cubed-proportional-to-period-squared law lets engineers choose a satellite's altitude to set its period. For a geostationary satellite, the altitude is chosen so the period equals one Earth day, keeping it fixed above a single point on the equator for TV, weather and navigation.

questions.q: State Kepler's three laws of planetary motion in the order he discovered them, as described in the episode.
keyPoints: First law: planetary orbits are ellipses (gentle ovals), not circles, with the sun sitting slightly off to one side (at a focus)
Second law: a planet speeds up when it swings close to the sun and slows down when it drifts far away
Third law: the cube of a planet's mean distance from the sun is directly proportional to the square of its orbital period (r³ ∝ T²), giving the same constant for every planet
The third law was the prize — a single rule tying ALL the planets together, not a separate law for each
questions.explanation: Kepler first cracked the shape (ellipses, first law), then how a planet's speed varies around its orbit (second law), and finally the single relationship binding every planet's distance to its period (third law). The third was the one he was really hunting: one law for the entire solar system at once.
